title: Wren and the Salt
premise: Orsen Iversen, a bone-carver who hears the dead through the things he carves, keeps the ledgers of the Salt Guild, which trades in impossible commodities: borrowed years, stolen names, memories pressed into salt. When a dying stranger presses a map into his hands and dies whispering the king's true name, Orsen discovers the crown on the throne is not an object but a hunger — a thing that eats its wearer's memory and wears him like a glove. Guided by the map and by the dead who refuse to stay quiet, Orsen must reach the capital before the king forgets himself entirely, unbind the crown, and choose whether to inherit the guild's terrible ledger or burn it. In the end he frees the king by giving the crown his own name to chew on — and walks away half-remembered, carving a new life from what remains.
about_author: Cyrus Yarrow is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the belongings of the unclaimed dead. They write fantasy about inheritance, grief, and the objects that outlive us.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Impossible Things
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. In the Salt Guild's counting house, Orsen carves a bone token for a widow buying back one hour of her husband's voice, establishing how the trade works and how the dead speak to him through his work. His mentor, Guildmistress Vess, warns him never to ask where the salt comes from. The beat is quiet unease — a man comfortable in a morally gray world.

chapters.title: A Stranger at Low Tide
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. A half-drowned stranger collapses into the guild's doorway, presses a salt-stiffened map into Orsen's hands, and dies naming the king. The corpse's bones, when Orsen touches them, scream. Vess orders the map surrendered to the guild; Orsen lies for the first time in his life. The beat is complicity — the moment the story hooks into him.

chapters.title: What the Bones Remember
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Working the stranger's femur secretly, Orsen recovers fragments of memory: a road north, a tower of white salt, a man in a crown begging to be forgotten. Guild enforcers search his rooms; he hides the map inside a carved bone he cannot hear — the only silent object he's ever made. The beat is dread sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Road That Isn't on Any Map
chapters.summary: POV alternating Orsen and the stranger's lingering echo, who rides as a voice in the carved bone. Orsen flees the city along a tidal road that exists only at certain hours. The echo, Nell, remembers dying and resents being a passenger. Their friction establishes the book's central question: who owns a memory? The beat is wary partnership.

chapters.title: Saltmarket
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. In a border town where the guild buys memories wholesale from the desperate, Orsen sees the trade's human cost: children sold their own birthdays, an old woman who no longer knows her son. He meets Tam, a guild defector who recognizes the map and reveals the crown has worn four kings already. The beat is moral awakening.

chapters.title: The Thing Wearing the Crown
chapters.summary: POV shifting to King Aldric, lucid for one hour a day, writing letters to himself he will not remember sending. Through his eyes we see the crown's hunger from inside: it trades his childhood for decrees, his wife's face for alliances. His final coherent act is sealing a plea for help. The beat is tragedy — the enemy is also the victim.

chapters.title: Vess Comes Collecting
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Guildmistress Vess catches up with them, and we learn she sold her own past to rise within the guild — she literally does not know why she protects Orsen, only that some carved remnant of herself insists on it. She offers him his old life back if he surrenders the map. The beat is betrayal braided with love.

chapters.title: The Tower of White Salt
chapters.summary: POV Orsen and Aldric converging. Orsen reaches the salt tower beneath the palace where the crown was first mined from a drowned god's grave; Nell's echo grows fainter as they near it, because the salt drinks the dead. Aldric, nearly empty, mistakes Orsen for his son. The beat is grief at the threshold of the climax.

chapters.title: Unbinding
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Climax: Orsen offers the crown a bargain in the guild's own language of debt — a name more nourishing than a king's. He speaks his own. The crown releases Aldric and begins consuming Orsen's identity while Nell and the freed dead swarm it, overfeeding it, cracking it. Vess arrives and chooses, finally, to remember why she came. The beat is sacrifice.

chapters.title: Half-Remembered
chapters.summary: POV Orsen, fragmented then steadying. Aldric, restored but diminished, abolishes the memory trade; Orsen survives with gaps — he keeps Nell's name but loses his mother's face. He burns the ledger, keeps one blank page, and opens a small shop carving ordinary things that say nothing at all. Final image: a child asks what his scarred hands used to make. The beat is bittersweet renewal.
